sections.description: Introduces the patient, presenting symptoms, vital signs, and initial physical findings, emphasizing the clues that prompt a broad differential diagnosis.
subtopics: Demographic data and relevant past medical history (type 2 diabetes, lifestyle)
Chronology of symptoms: fever, headache, malaise, hiccups, arthralgia, oral aphthae
Physical examination findings: mucocutaneous lesions, neurologic status, volume status
Initial laboratory panel highlighting hyponatraemia, inflammation markers, CK elevation
First imaging studies (CT, chest X‑ray) and their negative results

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: From Differential Diagnosis to Definitive Diagnosis
sections.description: Explores the systematic approach to narrowing the differential, interpreting key investigations, and applying diagnostic criteria for Behçet’s disease, neuro‑Behçet’s disease, and SIADH.
subtopics: Formulating a differential for fever, headache, and hyponatraemia (infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic, endocrine)
Interpretation of CSF analysis: aseptic meningitis pattern, exclusion of viral/bacterial pathogens
Role of brain MRI findings (or lack thereof) in neuro‑Behçet’s disease
Application of International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease (point system, mucocutaneous signs, HLA‑B51)
Diagnostic criteria for acute neuro‑Behçet’s disease (clinical CNS involvement + exclusion of other causes)
Diagnostic work‑up for SIADH (serum/urine osmolality, urinary Na, ADH levels, exclusion of volume depletion, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency)
Rationale for ruling out sarcoidosis, lymphoma, other autoimmune disorders

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology Linking Neuro‑Behçet’s Disease and SIADH
sections.description: Provides a concise review of the immunologic mechanisms of Behçet’s disease, CNS inflammation, and how cytokine‑mediated processes can trigger inappropriate ADH secretion.
subtopics: Overview of Behçet’s disease: vasculitis, neutrophil hyperactivity, IL‑6 and IL‑1β role
Acute neuro‑Behçet’s disease: meningoencephalitis, typical brainstem involvement, CSF cytokine profile
Mechanisms of SIADH in CNS inflammation: hypothalamic‑pituitary axis disturbance, cytokine‑induced ADH release (focus on IL‑6)
Potential contribution of systemic inflammation (high CRP) to ADH dysregulation
Why SIADH is rare in BD and the importance of recognizing this association

sections.description: Details the step‑wise treatment decisions, monitoring strategies, and outcomes, highlighting the unique use of colchicine monotherapy and SIADH management.
subtopics: Empiric antimicrobial therapy: indications, agents used, and de‑escalation
Antiviral coverage and its withdrawal after negative viral studies
Initiation of colchicine: dosing, mechanism of action relevant to BD and neuro‑inflammation
Supportive care for SIADH: fluid restriction protocol, sodium monitoring, avoidance of rapid correction
Adjunctive topical therapies for mucocutaneous lesions
Timeline of clinical improvement: fever resolution, neurologic symptom abatement, normalization of sodium and ADH
Rationale for not using corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants

sections.description: Synthesizes key teaching points, emphasizes pitfalls, and suggests areas for further research or clinical vigilance.
subtopics: Recognition that neuro‑Behçet’s disease can present concurrently with systemic disease
Importance of evaluating hyponatraemia in patients with CNS symptoms – SIADH as a red flag
Potential role of colchicine as frontline therapy in selected acute neuro‑BD cases
Monitoring for complications of hyponatraemia (hiccups, rhabdomyolysis) and early intervention
Limitations of current evidence: need for prospective studies on colchicine monotherapy and IL‑6 driven SIADH in BD
Practical algorithm for clinicians faced with fever, headache, mucocutaneous lesions, and hyponatraemia
